sections.overview: The chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) is a great ape native to tropical Africa. It differs from the bonobo (Pan paniscus), found south of the Congo River; chimpanzees live north of it. This adaptable, social omnivore climbs and travels on the ground, and learns local traditions.
sections.identification: Adults have long arms, a robust build and dark brown to black hair; the face, palms and soles are bare. They have no tail, walk on their knuckles and climb readily. Males are generally larger than females, and coat shade varies. Adult head-to-rump length is about 0.9 m; San Diego Zoo reports masses of 32–45 kg for females and 40–55 kg for males, with males generally larger.
sections.habitat: The range runs from West Africa to western Uganda and Tanzania, interrupted by the Congo basin of the bonobo. Chimpanzees inhabit rainforests, dry forests, woodland-savanna mosaics and mountain forests. Some populations also live in open savanna, so the species is not restricted to dense forest.
sections.diet: Fruit is often a major food, alongside leaves, seeds, flowers, bark, honey and insects; the mix varies by season and place. Chimpanzees also hunt or scavenge vertebrates such as monkeys and small antelopes. Some use probes at termite mounds or tools to fish for ants; techniques vary among communities.
sections.behavior: Communities have a fission-fusion structure: members split into flexible parties and reunite. Males usually stay in their birth community; females may transfer. Grooming, calls, gestures and alliances maintain ties. Tool practices learned socially differ locally: neighbouring groups at Gombe, Tanzania, make different tools for termite fishing.
sections.reproduction: After about 7½ to 8½ months, a female usually gives birth to one infant. It clings to her and remains dependent for years; nursing often lasts three to four years, followed by continued travel and learning with its mother. This long care period spaces births, though timing varies.
sections.ecology: Eating fruit and travelling through forests can disperse seeds; hunting affects prey, including red colobus at Gombe. These effects depend on local foods, prey and habitat. Tools also give access to insects and other hard-to-reach resources.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List’s 2016 global assessment classified the species as Endangered, citing decline from hunting, habitat loss and degradation, and disease. This is the date of that assessment, not a new population count.
